exercises.title: Counting pets per owner
exercises.prompt:
A small town's animal licensing office keeps two small tables instead of one big spreadsheet. `owners` has one row per registered pet owner: a unique `owner_id` and a `name`. `pets` has one row per licensed pet: its own `pet_id`, a `name`, and an `owner_id` that must match a real row in `owners` - that matching link is the whole point of splitting the data into two tables instead of retyping the owner's details on every pet row.

owners

| owner_id | name |
|---|---|
| 1 | Farah |
| 2 | Bilal |
| 3 | Mina |

pets

| pet_id | name | owner_id |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Milo | 1 |
| 11 | Coco | 2 |
| 12 | Rex | 1 |
| 13 | Nala | 3 |
| 14 | Simba | 2 |
| 15 | Leo | 2 |

Example: Farah's `owner_id` is 1, and two `pets` rows have `owner_id` 1 (Milo, Rex), so Farah owns 2 pets.

How many pets does Bilal own? Answer with a single number.
exercises.starterCode: -- No query to write here. Read the two tables above, then type your numeric answer in the response box.
exercises.referenceSolution: Bilal's owner_id is 2. Scanning the pets table for rows where owner_id equals 2 finds Coco, Simba, and Leo, so Bilal owns 3 pets. The link only works because every owner_id value in pets matches a real owner_id in owners - that is exactly what a foreign key guarantees, and it is why two small linked tables can stand in for one repetitive spreadsheet.

exercises.title: Two identical library loans
exercises.prompt:
A neighborhood library tracks every loan in a single spreadsheet called Loans, with columns book_title, borrower_name, borrower_email, and loan_date. Nothing in the sheet guarantees that any row is different from any other row.

Loans

| book_title | borrower_name | borrower_email | loan_date |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Hobbit | Amal Hassan | amal@example.com | 2026-01-03 |
| Dune | Yousef Al-Sayed | yousef@example.com | 2026-01-04 |
| The Hobbit | Amal Hassan | amal@example.com | 2026-01-03 |
| 1984 | Reem Nasser | reem@example.com | 2026-01-05 |
| Dune | Yousef Al-Sayed | yousef@example.com | 2026-01-06 |

Rows 1 and 3 are word-for-word identical - maybe the library owns two copies of The Hobbit and both went out that day - but the sheet cannot tell those two loans apart. The librarian wants to add exactly one new column so every row is guaranteed different from every other row, and any single row can be looked up or corrected without touching the rest.

What is the two-word database term for that kind of column?
exercises.starterCode: -- No query to write here. Study the sheet above, then type your answer in the response box.
exercises.referenceSolution: Rows 1 and 3 have the exact same title, borrower, email, and loan date, so nothing in the sheet can tell them apart if the library ever needs to update or delete just one of them. Adding a primary key - a column such as loan_id that is unique for every row - fixes this: each loan gets its own id, so staff can act on one record without touching the other. A plain spreadsheet has no way to guarantee that on its own.

exercises.title: Turning an order sheet into tables
exercises.prompt:
Sunrise Bakery keeps one spreadsheet called Order Sheet with columns sale_id, customer_name, customer_phone, item_name, item_price, quantity, and sale_date. Every sale retypes the customer's name, phone, and the item's price, even when the same customer or item already appears on ten other rows.

The owner wants to split this into linked tables and has written five steps, but mixed up the order:

A. Add a foreign key column to the sales table for each table it must reference, so one sale points at one customer and one item.
B. Look at the sheet and list the separate things hiding inside it: customers, items, and sales.
C. Give each new table a primary key: a column guaranteed unique for every row in it.
D. For each thing, keep only the columns that describe it, moving item_price into its own table.
E. Create the tables, now that every table, key, and link between tables has been decided.

Answer with the five letters in the order the steps must happen, separated by a comma and a space, such as: A, B, C, D, E (a format example only, not the answer).
exercises.starterCode: -- No query to write here. Read the five steps above, then type your ordering in the response box.
exercises.referenceSolution: Start by finding the separate things hiding in the sheet - customers, items, and sales (B). Next, sort the columns so each of those things keeps only the columns that describe it, pulling item_price into its own items table (D). Only once a table's own columns are settled can it get a primary key that is guaranteed unique per row (C). A foreign key can only point at a primary key that already exists, so linking sales to customers and items comes next (A). Finally, with every table, key, and link decided, the tables themselves get created (E). Order: B, D, C, A, E.

exercises.title: Departments beating their own average
exercises.prompt:
A company's HR system already keeps two tables so a department's name and budget are never retyped for each employee: `departments(department_id, department_name, department_budget)` and `employees(employee_id, employee_name, department_id, salary)`.

HR wants a report built in three steps:

1. For each department, work out that department's own average salary.
2. Count how many of its employees earn strictly more than that average.
3. Keep only departments where that count is 2 or higher.

Write one query returning `department_name` and the count as `above_avg_count`, ordered by `above_avg_count` descending, then `department_name` ascending. A department with no employees never appears.

Example: if Engineering's four salaries average to 7675 and two of them (9000 and 8200) beat that average, Engineering's row shows `above_avg_count = 2`.
exercises.fixture:
create table departments (
  department_id integer primary key,
  department_name text,
  department_budget numeric
);
create table employees (
  employee_id integer primary key,
  employee_name text,
  department_id integer,
  salary numeric
);
insert into departments values
  (1,'Engineering',500000),
  (2,'Sales',200000),
  (3,'Support',150000),
  (4,'Research',100000);
insert into employees values
  (1,'Huda',1,9000),
  (2,'Omar',1,8200),
  (3,'Layla',1,7500),
  (4,'Zain',1,6000),
  (5,'Sara',2,6000),
  (6,'Fahad',2,5900),
  (7,'Reem',2,3000),
  (8,'Noor',3,4000),
  (9,'Kareem',3,3800);

tests.input:
select d.department_name, count(*) as above_avg_count
from employees e
join departments d on d.department_id = e.department_id
where e.salary > (
  select avg(e2.salary) from employees e2 where e2.department_id = e.department_id
)
group by d.department_name
having count(*) >= 2
order by above_avg_count desc, d.department_name asc;
tests.name: example

tests.input: __STUDENT__
tests.name: your query

tests.input: __STUDENT__ /* after: insert into employees values (10,'Amina',3,1000) */
__STUDENT__ /* after: delete from employees where employee_id = 4 */
__STUDENT__ /* after: update employees set salary = 4500 where department_id = 3 */
__STUDENT__ /* after: insert into employees values (10,'Aziz',4,5000) */

exercises.referenceSolution:
select d.department_name, count(*) as above_avg_count

exercises.title: Heavy ingredient recipes
exercises.prompt:
A recipe app stores one document per recipe in a `recipes` collection. Each document has `name`, `cuisine`, `servings`, and an `ingredients` array, where every item in the array has its own `name`, `qty`, and `unit`.

Write a query that returns every recipe with at least one ingredient measured in grams (`unit` is `"g"`) whose `qty` is strictly over `200`. The gram unit and the over-200 amount must belong to the SAME ingredient line -- a recipe with `30` g of garlic and `500` ml of broth does not qualify, even though one line has the right unit and a different line has a big enough number.

Example: a recipe with a `600` g beef ingredient qualifies; a recipe with only a `200` g ingredient does not.
